findings.text: A 64 bit interrupt configuration register is viewed either as one raw value or as named fields. The common and generation specific views share the same arrangement with an eight bit vector at the low end, delivery mode and destination mode nearby, status and presence style flags that are read only, a trigger style flag that is read only, a mask flag that is writable, reserved gaps, and a 32 bit APIC identifier in the upper half.

Interrupt configuration field positions are architecturally fixed with the vector at bit zero, delivery mode at bit eight, destination mode at bit eleven, status at twelve, presence at thirteen, trigger at fifteen, mask at sixteen, and APIC identifier at thirty two, with matching narrow masks for the low fields and a full upper word mask for the identifier.

A scratch register is modeled as a union of one raw 64 bit value and several identical structured views for common and generation specific families. Each view exposes the whole width as a single writable scratch field, so all views are layout compatible.

The scratch facility has one base address and two nearby alias addresses whose numeric values depend on hardware generation. Newer generations share one address family while older generations share a different lower address family, with aliases spaced eight bytes apart. Every scratch field starts at bit zero and spans the full 64 bit width in all common and generation specific naming variants.

The virtual dynamic shared object descriptor records a data pointer and total size plus alternate instruction range and exception table range metadata with a pointer to the table. It also carries signed offsets for signal return trampolines, legacy system call entry, compatibility landing pads, and futex list unlock critical region boundaries for both 64 and 32 bit variants.

The shared object size is always a multiple of the page size, and the alternate and exception table base plus length pairs delimit subranges used for patching and fault handling rather than arbitrary pointers.

The architecture advertises three virtual clock modes covering the processor cycle counter and two paravirtual clocks, with explicit support indicated for the hypervisor clock mode. Time and clock resolution services are marked available. The mapping reserves six pages total with two trailing virtual clock pages whose start derives from the base, using offset zero for one paravirtual clock and offset one for the other.

A small always inline helper issues the random bytes system trap directly from virtual shared object context, passing caller buffer, length and flags through the normal trap registers and returning the kernel result value to the caller.

Each time related fallback helper forwards to the generic virtual shared object trap helper with two arguments. There are distinct fallbacks for current time of day, wall clock and resolution queries in both native and 32 bit compatibility timestamp forms, distinguished by the requested trap name and 64 bit naming suffix.

Paravirtual cycle reads are only trusted when a stable timestamp flag is present. The paravirtual read samples version guarded per CPU time information from the first virtual CPU under a retry loop and the hypervisor read consults a shared page; either path reports the largest unsigned value on failure and otherwise clears the sign bit so valid results are non negative.

Hardware counter selection prefers the ordered processor cycle counter masked to the positive range, then optionally consults paravirtual or hypervisor pages behind compiler barriers, and otherwise reports the largest unsigned value. The architecture clock source check unconditionally approves, while a cycle value is deemed usable exactly when its signed interpretation is not negative.

Nanosecond conversion measures elapsed cycles since the last reference and scales by a multiplier plus base with a right shift. Oversized unsigned deltas take a slow path that suppresses values indicating backward motion and that safely handles multiply overflow with a masked wide multiply add shift helper, while normal deltas use direct scaled arithmetic.

Virtual shared object traps bind zero to five caller arguments to fixed argument registers and invoke an architecture trap instruction that returns its result through the accumulator register. The 64 bit form uses the fast system call instruction with caller saved registers clobbered, while the 32 bit form selects between a legacy interrupt sequence and a kernel entry call based on a fast system call feature, with different register assignment and trap number construction.

Module version magic carries a processor family tag selected at build time from a fixed set of seventeen alternatives covering early 586 classes through later Pentium, K6 and K7, Transmeta, Cyrix, VIA and Geode families. One build configuration exposes the selected family tag as the architecture version suffix while the other configuration exposes an empty suffix.

Legacy display memory mapping converts a supplied physical address to its kernel virtual address and, when encrypted memory support is enabled, marks the covered pages decrypted before returning the start address. Single byte display access is a direct volatile style load or store through the supplied pointer. Framebuffer protection and primary device queries are self defined aliases indicating architecture provided implementations.

Virtual 8086 register state extends the normal register frame with paired segment values and padding for the four data segments. The per task virtual 8086 container records a user pointer, a saved 32 bit register frame, extended flags and mask, saved stack pointer, control flags, CPU type, two bitmaps for redirected interrupts, and an information block for extensions.

Only interrupt numbers three through fifteen are considered valid for virtual 8086 redirection, with a helper reporting numbers outside that closed interval as invalid. One lifecycle helper releases attached virtual 8086 state and clears the owner pointer when present, while an alternate configuration defines fault handling, trap handling, state saving, interrupt release and freeing as no operation stubs returning success.

Default virtualization hooks do nothing on initialization and report absence when asked to disable virtualization on the calling CPU. Large mapping support for the virtual allocator is gated on processor capabilities, with one level requiring large page support and the other requiring page size extension support. The emergency virtualization callback is a parameterless procedure type.

Compiler reordering around the virtual clock mode check can cause an access to a disabled memory mapped clock page and therefore a fault, so the paravirtual paths require an ordering barrier after the mode test. Unstable paravirtual time, failed hypervisor reads, negative appearing cycles, backward processor counter motion, and multiply overflow must all be treated as invalid or clamped rather than used directly for time.
